title: IMF to Jim: Show ‘more ambition’
full_text:
The International Monetary Fund has implored Jim Chalmers and state treasurers to tighten their fiscal positions, redouble efforts to lift productivity, and enact wider tax reform amid the highest costs of Australian government debt in 15 years and stubbornly high inflation.
The Washington-based fund said “more ambitious” reform strategy was needed to lift productivity, which has crashed to an annual growth rate of -0.2 per cent, and faced downgrades from Treasury, the Reserve Bank and business groups. It also raised concerns about inflation risks from the energy-thirsty artificial-intelligence and digital-infrastructure boom.
The IMF also expects GDP growth to slow in the second half of this year, bringing the annual rate to 1.9 per cent in 2026 and to 1.6 per cent in 2027, with inflation to remain elevated this year.
After federal government debt hit more than $1 trillion last month, the Treasurer told parliament that rising rates would mean the country faced a higher interest bill, which had been forecast in the May budget to hit $29.5bn this year, or 1 per cent of GDP.
Australia’s 10-year government bond yield this week hit a 15-year high of 5.41 per cent and has surged 0.63 percentage points in 2½ months, adding to the IMF’s warnings about the rising cost of government spending.
“With public debt and interest costs rising, particularly in some states, a gradual tightening of the fiscal stance would help rebuild buffers,” the IMF said in its latest report on Australia.
“Public spending has increased steadily since the global financial crisis, and greater efforts will be needed to contain spending growth by strengthening efficiency and prioritisation.
“The combined fiscal deficit of the commonwealth and state governments widened over the past two fiscal years, reflecting large infrastructure investment by states, rising social spending, especially healthcare and the National Disability Insurance scheme, and response to the global energy price shock.” It said efforts to restrain government spending – which at the federal level will hit 26.8 per cent of GDP this year (the highest since 1986 outside the pandemic) – would “support disinflation efforts by the RBA”.
The IMF said overall public debt was relatively low compared with other advanced economies and praised Labor’s actions to control the growth of the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Its Australian mission chief, Paulo Medas, on Thursday identified the Iranian energy price shock and strong domestic demand as the primary drivers of inflation, again calling on the government to tighten spending. “It will be key to slow down domestic demand, and in our view, if fiscal policy tightens that will help because it reduces domestic demand,” Mr Medas said in Sydney. “I think at this stage, we have talked to the commonwealth and the states. There is an intention to contain spending growth … If they do that, that will help reduce inflation.” While warning on fiscal consolidation, the IMF also made strong recommendations on productivity and tax reform.
“The authorities’ focus on productivity is welcome, but a more ambitious reform strategy is needed,” it said. “One key challenge is to better balance growth with other policy objectives when introducing new regulations. Further progress on smarter regulation, alongside addressing infrastructure bottlenecks and making the tax system more growth-friendly, would help boost productivity. The weaker performance has been across many sectors, as business dynamism has weakened, also reflecting regulatory creep and fragmented regulations across states. Reversing the productivity slowdown will be crucial to improving living standards and healthy public and private balance sheets.” Australia’s biggest employers this week went to war with the government over tax, industrial relations and red tape strangling the economy, after data revealed Dr Chalmers would deliver the worst decade of productivity since records began in 1960.
The IMF said tax changes in the May budget would help some property buyers but compliance costs could be damaging, and suggested there needed to be more comprehensive tax reform. “Recent changes to capital gains taxation and negative gearing can reduce housing-related distortions, but continued efforts to minimise compliance costs and impact on investment are needed during implementation,” it warned. “Over time a comprehensive tax reform could help promote economic growth and sustainability of public finances. Such reform could involve replacing stamp duties with recurrent property taxes, broadening the tax base – for example, consumption tax – and reducing reliance on income taxes.” The Treasurer said he took the latest IMF recommendations seriously. “Our responsible economic management is more important than ever with all the uncertainty and volatility in the world,” Dr Chalmers said. “The IMF’s statement highlights Australia’s relative economic strengths and the importance of our ambitious reform agenda.” Dr Chalmers noted the IMF’s warnings on AI and data centres.
“Major shifts, like the AI revolution, will be front and centre of the Intergenerational Report I release next week, which is all about how we’re making Australians the beneficiaries not victims of all this change,” he said.
The IMF said AI and digital infrastructure could be a new source of growth, but contained plenty of risks. “Rising investment in data centres also poses policy challenges from both cyclic and structural perspectives that will need to be managed,” it said. “It is already putting pressure on the construction sector and could lead to higher energy costs if renewable energy expansion lags, ultimately leading to higher inflation.” Estimates by Goldman Sachs economist Andrew Boak show Australia could benefit from $130bn of cumulative investment in data centres and related infrastructure through to 2029-30.
The Albanese government last month backed down on its threat to tap constitutional powers to enforce the data-centre industry to be fuelled entirely by renewable power sources.
Opposition Treasury spokesman Tim Wilson said the IMF had showed the failure of the government’s economic model. “The IMF has called out the Albanese government in pursuing higher taxes, higher debt and smashing confidence for investment and improvement of the wealth and wages of Australians”, he said.
